title: Year three close: the long story is yours
hook: from the apostles to now, saints and sinners, and now your chapter

segments.voice: Yesterday, hagioi, Paul's word for holiness close by. Your line was the saint next door. Did you send that message? Today, the last day of year three. Day one thousand sixty-one.

The Acts of the Apostles doesn't end the way a book usually ends. Paul is in Rome, under guard in a rented house, and people keep coming to see him. There's no trial verdict, no farewell, no last scene. Luke just stops, with Paul still talking. Some readers have wondered why. This year began right there, at the edge of that unfinished page, and asked: what happened next? Today we look back at the answer, and find out whose turn it is.
screen: `ACTS STOPS MID-STORY.` → `PAUL STILL TALKING IN ROME.` → `WHAT HAPPENED NEXT?`

segments.voice: Here's how Acts ends, in the Douay-Rheims. Paul is preaching the kingdom of God "with all confidence, without prohibition." Then nothing. The story spills off the page. Year three picked it up. First, the first Christians and the Fathers: Peter and Paul in Rome, a fish scratched on a catacomb wall, martyrs and bishops and the great teachers. Second, the councils: bishops arguing out who Christ is, and the words of the creed said at Sunday Mass. Third, the middle ages: monastery bells, bread and books, reformers, builders, a church trying to tame knights. Fourth, reform, mission and revolution: a soldier with a smashed leg reading saints' lives in bed, missionaries crossing oceans, a Church shaken and renewed. Fifth, the modern Church: a parish priest hearing confessions for hours on end, an Oxford scholar following his conscience, councils and popes facing a new world. And then the saints across the calendar, day by day, ending yesterday with the ones next door. This year opened with a line: saints and sinners, both. The Church's history isn't a parade of heroes. It holds martyrs and cowards, reformers and the people who needed reforming, a king's friend killed in his own cathedral. The Church has even asked forgiveness, in public, for sins committed by its own members. And Catholic teaching holds that God kept working through all of it, through weak people as well as strong ones. That's the carry. If Acts ends mid-story, then the generations since have been writing the next line. The story the Church tells about itself is still being written, by people alive now. And whoever is listening has a chapter of their own, whatever they make of that older story.
screen: `WITH ALL CONFIDENCE, WITHOUT PROHIBITION.` · `FATHERS, COUNCILS, MIDDLE AGES.` · `REFORM, MISSION, THE MODERN CHURCH.` · `SAINTS AND SINNERS, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own chapter. Find a pen and a scrap of paper, or your phone. Settle, and breathe. Let this year pass by: the people you met in these lessons, and the people in your own life. Then ask one question: if someone wrote down this year of mine, what is one true sentence they'd want to include? Not a resolution. Not a speech. One honest line about where you are. Write it. If you pray, you can hold it up to God as part of the longer story. If you don't, just keep it somewhere you'll find it next year. The bell holds the time.

Acts. The book that ends mid-story, in Rome, with Paul still talking; from there, the first Christians, the councils, and the saints across the calendar, kept honestly, saints and sinners both, and still being written. Today's word.
Your line: your chapter. Today, put the sentence you wrote somewhere you'll see it, a drawer, a book, a note on your phone, and read it once more before you sleep. Day one thousand sixty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Church's history alive through the calendar of saints, the readings at Mass and the lives of the saints, and some families keep notes of their own faith story alongside it.
